28095.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse júði (“Jew”), reshaped after Middle Low German jode (“Jew”) (also jude (“Jew”)). Both forms ultimately derive from Latin iūdaeus (“Jew; Jewish”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos, “Judaean; Jew”), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yəhūḏā, “Judah”). The underlying ethnonym originally referred to a member of the tribe of Judah and was later extended to the Jewish people.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk jøde, Danish jøde, Swedish jude, German Jude and English Jew.
